content_metadata.description: A piece from 'The Rachel Maddow Show' discussing tax disparities between the wealthy and average Americans, corporate tax avoidance, and the potential of a financial transaction tax, alongside insights from Michael Moore on the Occupy Wall Street movement.

qAndA.question: What was Warren Buffett's total tax rate?
What percentage did the average person in Warren Buffet's office pay in taxes?
How much did the 30 Fortune 500 companies discussed make in profit over the three years?

qAndA.answer: People making $40,000 a year pay 7% of their income to Social Security, while wealthy people pay 0% after their income surpasses $110,000.
qAndA.question: Why does Michael Moore say the wealthy should pay a Social Security tax on all of their income?

qAndA.answer: Michael Moore feels very optimistic about the movement's future because it already has the support of tens of millions of Americans.
qAndA.question: How does Michael Moore feel about the future of the Occupy Wall Street movement?

A red border on the bottom left with the abbreviation 'TRMS.'

A banner at the top right with the text 'LEAN FORWARD' appears.

activities.description: Rachel Maddow speaks about a new report showing corporations paying less than zero percent in taxes.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Rachel Maddow aims to raise awareness of corporate tax avoidance and its impact on average Americans.

mood.description: Angry. Rachel Maddow speaks with a critical and indignant tone.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Transition from research paper visual to an aerial photograph of a polluted lake.

narrativeProgression.description: Rachel Maddow discusses a report showing how some major companies paid no federal income tax, even while making billions of dollars in profit.
Rachel Maddow states that at least 30 Fortune 500 companies paid zero taxes or less in the last 3 years.
Rachel Maddow explains that those companies made $160 billion in profit.
Rachel Maddow describes a company that dumped pollution into Lake Michigan and still paid less taxes than many individuals.

props.name: A research paper titled “Corporate Taxpayers & Corporate Tax Dodgers 2008-10" appears on the screen.

scenes.title: Rachel Maddow on Corporate Tax Avoidance

videoEditingDetails.description: A blue border at the top of the video with the names 'RACHEL MADDOW SHOW' and 'MSNBC' appear.
A red border on the bottom left with the abbreviation 'TRMS.'
The text '30 companies paid less than zero percent [from 2008-2010]…' is superimposed on the research paper.
The text 'U.S. profits totaled $160 billion over the three years…' is superimposed on the research paper.

activities.description: Rachel Maddow introduces Bill Gates’ advocacy for a financial transaction tax.
Bill Gates speaks in an interview about the concept of a financial transaction tax.
Rachel Maddow mentions various groups and individuals who support a financial transaction tax, including National Nurses United, Democrats in Congress, the Archbishop of Canterbury, and the Pope.
Rachel Maddow explains that Angela Merkel and Nicolas Sarkozy are also in favor of the tax and have discussed it with President Obama.
Rachel Maddow talks about President Obama’s previous support for the tax and how Lawrence Summers reportedly pushed against it within the administration.
Rachel Maddow notes that the US officially does not support a global financial transaction tax despite its allies supporting it.

characterInteraction.description: Rachel Maddow presents information about Bill Gates, the Pope, Angela Merkel, Nicolas Sarkozy, Barack Obama, and Lawrence Summers.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Rachel Maddow showcases the growing momentum and support for this tax from unexpected sources, contrasting it with US opposition, raising questions about whose interests are being served.

mood.description: Hopeful. Rachel Maddow’s tone is more optimistic, discussing the possibility of a new tax. Bill Gates speaks in a positive and hopeful tone.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Transition from optimistic discussion of the tax to mentioning the US opposition, shifting the mood slightly towards disappointment.

narrativeProgression.description: Rachel Maddow explains that Bill Gates has called on the G20 to support a financial transaction tax. This tax is supported by diverse groups and individuals globally, including the Pope and Angela Merkel. While President Obama previously supported it, Lawrence Summers allegedly blocked it. Despite this setback, Rachel Maddow suggests it may still be possible.
Bill Gates defines a financial transaction tax as a 'very, very small tax,' around 0.25%.
The Archbishop of Canterbury and the Pope are mentioned as supporters of the tax.
The US government is noted as not officially supporting the tax.

scenes.thematicElements: Financial transaction tax, global efforts to address economic inequality.
scenes.title: Global Push for a Financial Transaction Tax

videoEditingDetails.description: Footage of Bill Gates entering the G20 summit.
A shot of Bill Gates speaking in an interview.
Footage of National Nurses United protesting in Washington, D.C., with a banner that reads 'HEAL AMERICA TAX WALL STREET.'
Images of three Democratic Congressman at a podium, the Archbishop of Canterbury, and the Pope appear in succession.
Images of Angela Merkel and Nicolas Sarkozy appear, followed by footage of them speaking with Barack Obama at the G20 summit.
Footage of Barack Obama and Australian Prime Minister Kevin Rudd speaking at a podium.

activities.description: Rachel Maddow transitions to an interview with Michael Moore.
Michael Moore discusses his support for a financial transaction tax and the potential of the Occupy Wall Street movement.

characterInteraction.description: Rachel Maddow engages in a conversational interview with Michael Moore.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Michael Moore argues that the current moment presents a unique opportunity for positive change, citing public support for the Occupy Wall Street movement and the feasibility of a financial transaction tax.

mood.description: Optimistic. Both Rachel Maddow and Michael Moore express a hopeful outlook.

narrativeProgression.description: Rachel Maddow interviews Michael Moore about his perspective on a financial transaction tax and the potential impact of the Occupy Wall Street movement. Michael Moore argues that a financial transaction tax would be a simple and effective way to raise revenue and that the Occupy Wall Street movement has widespread public support and potential for achieving its goals.
Rachel Maddow thanks Michael Moore for sticking around.
Michael Moore explains the tax as “a half a penny or a quarter of a penny per dollar that’s traded on the stock market.”
Michael Moore says that the tax would raise “a minimum of $350 billion dollars a year of extra income.”
Michael Moore reminds viewers that the Occupy Wall Street movement is 'only six weeks old.'

scenes.thematicElements: Financial transaction tax, Occupy Wall Street movement, political activism.
scenes.title: Michael Moore on Financial Reform and Activism

videoEditingDetails.description: A split-screen format with Rachel Maddow on the left and Michael Moore on the right.
The text 'THE INTERVIEW' is displayed on the bottom left.
A banner with 'MICHAEL MOORE, AUTHOR, ‘HERE COMES TROUBLE’' appears at the bottom.
A banner with 'MICHAEL MOORE, ACADEMY AWARD WINNING FILMMAKER' appears at the bottom.

climax.description: The climax points out the disparity in tax obligations and the wide-reaching support yet governmental opposition to proposed financial reforms.

storylines.description: The video explores the themes of tax disparities, corporate tax avoidance, support for a financial transaction tax, and the potential impact of the Occupy Wall Street movement.

content_metadata.title: The Rachel Maddow Show: Analyzing Wealth and Taxes
